title: Why don't we have words for these things?

entries.note: A word that could exist, since grammar and sound patterns allow it, but doesn't; gaps can be sound-based, like [[see:sprick]], or meaning-based.
Given by Jess as another name for a [[see:lexical gap]].
A possible but nonexistent word made from spr- and -ick; the hosts decide it should mean a springy stick for throwing a ball for a dog.
Jess's only word for a ball-throwing stick, which she thinks is a brand name; the hosts imagine it becoming generic.
A neologism coined as a gender-neutral word for a niece or nephew, filling a lexical gap.
Its etymology literally means new word.
Rob says it doesn't really work for his sister's husband's family, since his brother-in-law's brother can't also be his brother-in-law.
Jess's joke coinage for more distant [[see:in-law]]s.
Rob's joke extension of [[see:outlaws]] for in-laws you've never even met.
Jess's further joke variation on [[see:outlaws]] and [[see:yonder laws]].
Swedish for your father's brother, almost a portmanteau; English can't distinguish paternal from maternal uncles.
Swedish for your father's sister, paired with [[see:farbror]].
Swedish for your mother's brother, contrasted with [[see:farbror]].
Swedish for your mother's sister, contrasted with [[see:faster]].
A relatively recent coinage from psychology, one of the few English words for a mixed emotion.
Taking pleasure in someone else's pain; a German word that Rob says can now fairly be called English.
TV show whose German character wishes there were a word for enjoying someone else's misfortune, Jess's favourite joke about [[see:Schadenfreude]].
German for feeling someone else's shame.
The weight put on from comfort eating; Rob thinks grief fat would be a better translation.
Originally fear of being shut outside medieval city gates at night; now anxiety that time is running out for life goals. Jess links it to [[see:panic]].
From [[from:Pan]], god of the wilderness, which fits the idea of being trapped outside in [[see:Torschlusspanik]].
The closest English equivalent of [[equivalent:Torschlusspanik]], though it is more specific and takes two words.
A word combining parts from two language families, once considered bad form in English; [[see:Torschlusspanik]] is one, and German compounds produce them naturally.
Given as an English [[see:hybrid word]].
Given as an English [[see:hybrid word]].
Given as an English [[see:hybrid word]].
Reshaping a borrowed word so its foreign parts sound native, overlapping with [[see:folk etymology]], as in [[see:outrage]], [[see:muskrat]] and [[see:cockroach]].
A frequent topic in earlier episodes.
Not from out and rage but from French, from Latin [[from:ultraticum]], extraness; English reinterpreted it as a compound and respelled it.
From a Native American word more like [[from:musquash]], reshaped to look like an English word.
From a Native American word that sounded more like pacimon, reshaped to look Germanic or Latin-derived.
From Spanish [[from:cucaracha]], assimilated into English as two existing words that have nothing to do with the insect.
Passed from Arabic to Spanish, Italian and English, then was phono-semantically matched back into Levantine Arabic as [[gave:ardi shawki]].
Colloquial Levantine Arabic remodelling of [[from:artichoke]] used in Syria and Lebanon.
Japanese for empty orchestra, its ending being the Japanese assimilation of English [[from:orchestra]]; English then borrowed the word back.
The feeling of being away and wishing you were home; contrasted with [[see:Fernweh]], [[see:dépaysement]] and [[see:hiraeth]].
Already borrowed into English for a desire to get out and about; in German it specifically means being out in the hills, as in [[see:Wandern]], hiking.
A yearning to travel and be far away; the flip side of [[see:Heimweh]].
The feeling of strangeness at being somewhere other than home; not quite the same as [[see:homesickness]].
Usually Welsh people's longing for Wales, but more broadly a yearning for any absent person or thing; English has no single equivalent.
Latinised Greek for homecoming grief, coined by a Swiss medical student to translate [[from:Heimweh]]; an 1830s medical description helped move it into popular culture.
An earlier name for the condition called [[see:nostalgia]], thought to affect only Swiss soldiers and mercenaries abroad in the 1600s; probably PTSD.
What Rob says a similar PTSD-like condition was later called in England, compared with the [[see:Swiss disease]].
The original name for the condition later rendered as [[gave:nostalgia]]; the flip side of [[see:Fernweh]].
Drinking alone at home in your underwear with no intention of going out; it has become a bit of a meme.
In a 2023 episode, Homer claims he was doing [[see:kalsarikännit]] before it was fashionable.
Swedish for just the right amount, meaning ideal rather than merely sufficient like [[see:adequate]].
Contrasted with [[see:lagom]]: it means merely sufficient and has a slight negativity.
Danish coziness and more: being indoors by a roaring fire with friends and drink while it's cold outside.
Old English word for the dread or sadness before sunrise, apparently found only in the poem The Wife's Lament, about a woman who lost track of her exiled husband.
Old English had five or six words for kinds of witch, discussed in a spooky words episode; now there is essentially one word.
An Old English word for a kind of [[see:witch]], meaning poisoner, found in only one or two sources.
Another Old English word for a kind of [[see:witch]], perhaps meaning an enchantress.
Suggested as implying something slightly different from [[see:witch]].
A dialect word meaning to stare at someone's food hoping they'll give you some, as Jess's dogs do.
A possible noun English doesn't use beside arrival, although recital has the pair recitation.
A possible noun English doesn't use beside refusal, although proposal has the pair proposition.
Used where English lacks approvation; taken wholesale from Latin with its -tion ending, so the v of approval appears as a Latin b.
Creating a word by removing an apparent affix, often making verbs from Latin-derived -tion nouns borrowed from French; discussed in earlier episodes.
A [[see:back-formation]] from [[from:escalator]], discussed before.
An example of a Latin-derived -tion noun adopted directly from French, with the verb made later.
Entered English after the noun evaluation, as a [[see:back-formation]].
Entered English after the noun regurgitation, as a [[see:back-formation]].
Entered English after the noun exploitation, as a [[see:back-formation]].
Entered English before its verb, giving [[gave:destruct]] by back-formation.
Adopted from Old French in the 1300s, about 400 years before its verb [[gave:resurrect]]; mentioned in an earlier episode.
Back-formed from [[from:resurrection]] 400 years later; deemed incorrect until the early 1900s because the Latin root suggests [[see:resurge]].
The verb a prescriptivist would form from the Latin root of [[see:resurrection]]; since it already existed, English made [[see:resurrect]] instead.
From Latin [[from:destruere]], to tear down or unbuild; the oldest of its group, arriving in the 1200s with Norman French spelling.
A back-formation from [[from:destruction]], not a verb until 1958, and less used because English already had [[see:destroy]].
Shares the Latin root [[from:struere]] with [[same-root:destroy]].
From Latin [[from:struere]] like [[same-root:destroy]]; made after the noun construction, so it keeps the -struct form.
From Latin [[from:struere]] like [[same-root:destroy]]; made after the noun obstruction, so it keeps the -struct form.
More common than plain [[see:destruct]]; first appeared in 1966 in the opening voiceover of Mission: Impossible.
A verb back-formed from the adjective [[from:sulky]].
An adjective back-formed from the noun [[from:grandiloquence]].
A back-formation younger than [[from:lazy]].
A back-formation younger than [[from:hesitation]].
A back-formation younger than [[from:editor]], discussed in an earlier episode.
The situation before a significant event; a joke formed from [[from:aftermath]] in a 1911 piece in Collier's.
A legitimate Indian English word meaning to move something forward, the counterpart of [[see:postpone]].
Invented as the opposite of the figurative sense of [[from:overwhelm]], which makes little sense given that [[see:whelm]] means to turn over; Rob covered it recently.
Literally to turn something over with great gusto, from [[from:whelm]]; figuratively to astonish.
Means to flip or turn something over.
Borrowed because English had no word of its own for the feeling.
Words like [[see:exuberant]] and [[see:ineffable]] that lack a counterpart; also called [[see:lost positives]] or [[see:orphan negatives]], discussed before.
Another name for [[see:unpaired words]].
Another name for [[see:unpaired words]].
One of the [[see:unpaired words]]: English has no uberant.
One of the [[see:unpaired words]]: English has no chalant.
English has improvise and provision but no verb provise.
English has no effable; Jess jokes that we just say eff it.
Inattentive, from [[from:gorm]], attention; one of Rob's favourite [[see:unpaired words]].
Meant attention: to take gorm was to pay attention, which gave [[gave:gormless]].
The hypothetical opposite of [[see:gormless]]: full of gorm, paying a great deal of attention.
Paired with archaic [[see:wist]]; came to suggest bittersweet melancholy or nostalgia through the term [[see:had I wist]].
An archaic word meaning to know, from Old English [[from:witan]] of the same meaning.
Middle and Early Modern English noun for regret over a rash action, especially in 'had I wist cometh ever too late'; it shaped [[see:wistful]].
Used instead of dorkity, since English tends to put Germanic suffixes on Germanic roots.
Used instead of kindity, keeping a Germanic suffix on a Germanic word.
Preferred over [[see:stupidness]] because it sounds and rolls better.
Used, as is wideness, while widity is rare.
Sounds odd to Rob, perhaps because it puts a Germanic suffix on a French word; [[see:stupidity]] sounds better.
An agent noun English doesn't use, though -er usually turns verbs like teach into nouns like teacher.
Not used for someone who lives because it already names an organ, leaving English with no word for a living person.
Rejected as a word for a living person because it only means someone who will die.
The closest English has to a word for a person who is alive, though the hosts joke about whether there could be a dead being.
Words like [[see:what's-it]] and [[see:doohickey]] filling in for an unknown or forgotten word; also called dummy words, fillers or [[see:kadigan]]s.
One of the [[see:placeholder names]] for something whose name you don't know or can't recall.
One of the [[see:placeholder names]] for something whose name you don't know or can't recall.
Another name for [[see:placeholder names]] of unknown origin, so itself a made-up word for made-up words.
One of the [[see:placeholder names]] for something whose name you don't know.
One of the [[see:placeholder names]] for something whose name you don't know.
A generic placeholder name, also a [[see:kadigan]] because it takes the place of a real name.
The female counterpart of [[see:John Doe]], a generic placeholder name.
A recurring fictional brand in Warner Bros. cartoons, ironic because it means the highest point, much to [[see:Wile E. Coyote]]'s dismay; real companies use it too.
Placeholder text that corrupts [[see:Cicero]]'s [[from:De finibus bonorum et malorum]] into gibberish; its name truncates [[from:dolorem ipsum]], pain itself.
A placeholder number, as in for the nth time or to the nth degree.
A placeholder for a remote town, from the [[from:Podunk people]] of marshy Connecticut near Hartford, in whose language it means a place where you sink in mire.
Used like [[see:Podunk]] for a generic distant place.
Once used for somewhere very far away.
The fake film director's name put in the credits when someone doesn't want to be credited; discussed in an earlier episode.
Originally a name for the average American soldier, before it named the toy and character.
Listed among the English [[see:placeholder names]] for people.
Listed among the English [[see:placeholder names]] for people.
Listed among the English [[see:placeholder names]] for people.
German placeholder name shown on sample ID and residency cards, its surname meaning template man; like [[see:Joe Bloggs]].
The English placeholder name Rob compares with [[see:Max Mustermann]].
A psycholinguistic test where children shown a made-up creature called a wug supply the plural wugs, showing they internalise morphology young.
Unfamiliar made-up words like those in the [[see:wug test]], showing that people apply grammatical forms to entirely new words.
A word, often funny, made up for an unnamed concept; coined by [[see:Barbara Wallraff]] of the Atlantic Monthly because they are wanted words.
A deliberately humorous word for something with no dictionary word, coined by [[see:Rich Hall]] in the early 1980s and introduced on HBO's [[see:Not Necessarily the News]].
The comedian who coined [[see:sniglet]]; Rob notes he is still alive, about 71, and popular in Britain.
A [[see:sniglet]], dork spelled with two Os, for a person who pushes on a door marked pull.
A [[see:sniglet]] for parking your car, walking away, then watching it roll past you.
A [[see:sniglet]] for an insult that, once called out, is excused as just a joke.
A [[see:sniglet]] for the pocket of air inside a potato chip bag.
A [[see:sniglet]] for turning on the bathtub tap with your toes; the hosts note it doesn't hold water etymologically, given [[see:ambidextrous]].
A [[see:sniglet]] for ice at the bottom of an upturned glass suddenly sliding toward your mouth; an ice [[from:avalanche]].

entries.term: Man Won't Stop Coming Up With New Sniglets
entries.note: A 2001 article in The Onion about a man still inventing [[see:sniglet]]s nearly 20 years after the fad, such as [[see:creamerass]] and [[see:snubbler]].
A [[see:sniglet]] from the Onion article for the non-dairy creamer residue at the bottom of a cup.
A [[see:sniglet]] from the Onion article for the pop-up safety button on juice-drink caps.
A comic new definition of an existing word, which Rob thinks came from the radio show [[see:I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue]], his favourite round.
Given the [[see:daffynition]] possessing only ten teeth.
Jess says [[see:sniglet]]s are really portmanteaus, like those [[see:Lewis Carroll]] created.
A [[see:sniglet]] from Jess and her co-workers for accidentally stumbling into a witticism mid-sentence.
A [[see:sniglet]] from Jess and her co-workers for an error that simplifies a process.
A [[see:sniglet]] from Jess and her co-workers for the moment every intelligent thing you planned to say leaves your mind.
Rebracketed in a joke redefinition as a flaming goblin.
Rebracketed in a joke redefinition as where one puts dirty dishes, in the sink; Rob finds it weak.
Rebracketed in a joke redefinition as how geese fly, in formation.
Rebracketed in a joke redefinition as Italian suppositories.
A [[see:word fugitive]] that Jess believes means anxiety about your phone alarm going off.
Originally a portmanteau by [[see:Lewis Carroll]] in [[see:Jabberwocky]] that caught on in ordinary, unironic use.
Originally a portmanteau by [[see:Lewis Carroll]] in [[see:Jabberwocky]] that caught on in ordinary, unironic use.
